journal.text: Undersexton Aveline Rell has given me a sealed quarterly return to carry from Soulrest to the Court's factor in Gideon. She pays a hundred and twenty in advance, which is more than the work is worth, and she asked twice whether anyone had spoken to me on the stair.

I put the return in the factor's hand in Gideon and said nothing about the man in the coat, and I was paid the rest of my hundred and twenty. Rell wrote something down when I told her the road had been quiet, and she did not believe me, and she hired me again anyway.

Rell wants eleven burial boxes counted and their weights written down. They came back from the wells at Bone Ladder and Salt-Egg Camp with nothing in them, which she says happens, and which she is nonetheless paying me to write down.

Eleven boxes, eleven weights, all of them the weight of an empty box. Rell read the list twice and put it in a press that already had a great many lists in it. I gave her the list and she did not thank me for it.

Rell wants to know why the sapwell at the Bone Ladder has stopped giving. She is not sending a rootkeeper and she is not sending a sexton. She is sending me, because I owe the wells nothing and because whatever is wrong there will not have any hold on me.

I told Rell the well had simply failed, because that was what she was paying to hear and because Teeja-Lun asked me to. The Court will send a rootkeeper in the spring and the rootkeeper will find the shaft, and it will not be me who told them.

Rell says I am becoming legible. A stranger who does nothing but errands for the Drowned Court is a stranger everyone can read, and she would rather I were harder to read than that. She wants me to take a name somewhere else — any name, she does not care which — so that when I am seen on a road there is another reason for it.
I have a name in the Wet Ledger now and a reason to be on the river that is not the Court's reason. Rell asked which one I had taken and then did not write it down, which I noticed.
Rell has sent for me to stand in the Court's chapter room while something is read out. She would not say what. She would only say that I should not answer anything I am asked until it is over.

I stood there and let them read it and said nothing, and afterwards the Court has a tally-reader and I have a name I did not ask for. Rell says the name is worth more than the money and she is not wrong, and I notice that she never said whether it is true.

Hosk-Vei has agreed to open the Tally to me, all four hundred years of it, on the condition that I read it in the room and write nothing down that I cannot say out loud to him first. He wants the same thing I want, which is a number.

The curve is thirty-six years old and the cutting licences are twenty-eight. I can say that now and mean it, and I can say who has been writing corrections into the return column since before anyone alive was born. Hosk-Vei asked me to say it out loud to him twice before he would let me leave with it.

lines.greeting: A prison town is the right town for this work. Nobody here asks where a soul came from.
lines.spellmaking: Writing a spell is a scribe's trade with the wind behind it. I am not a scribe. Gideon has one, and Gideon is four days upriver, and you will find the four days are part of what you are paying.
lines.enchanting: A hundred and ten points, and forty in the hundred over what a journeyman would ask. You are paying for the ceiling, not for the hands.

lines.greeting: The Court counts its dead and I count my points, and only one of those two counts is accurate.
lines.spellmaking: Not my trade. Lilmoth has a spellwright and Lilmoth is downriver of everything, which is the one convenient thing anybody has ever said about Lilmoth.
lines.enchanting: A hundred and ten. Bring the item whole; I will not enchant a thing that is already cracked, whatever you have been told in the market.

lines.greeting: Two brothers, one bed, and neither of them has paid. Sit anywhere but there.

The lease is up in seven months and no clerk in Cyrodiil has read the clause. Sit.
